title: arr[4294967295] = x does not grow a JavaScript array's length, but arr[4294967294] = x does
assumption: Any non-negative integer you assign as an array subscript is a real array index that updates .length.

input.display: arr[2**32 - 2] = "a" updates .length to 2**32 - 1; arr[2**32 - 1] = "b" does NOT update .length at all
input.description: Computing a very large array index programmatically (from a hash, an offset calculation, or a bug) and writing to it, expecting ordinary array growth semantics.

what_goes_wrong: Writing to what looks like 'one past the last valid huge index' silently creates an ordinary (non-index) property on the array object instead of extending the array, so `.length`, `for` loops bounded by `.length`, and array methods like `.forEach` never see that value at all.
why: The ECMAScript spec defines an 'array index' as a string that is a canonical numeric representation of an integer in the range 0 to 2^32 - 2 inclusive -- 2^32 - 1 is deliberately excluded, because an array's `.length` is always an integer from 0 to 2^32 - 1 (setting it to 2^32 throws `RangeError`) and must be able to hold 'one past the largest index'. So the largest valid index is 2^32 - 2; assigning to 2^32 - 1 is legal (arrays allow arbitrary property keys) but does not count as an array index and therefore never triggers the `.length`-update behavior that real index assignment does.

repros.expected_output:
after valid index: 4294967295
after 2**32 - 1: 4294967295
both keys present: true true
own enumerable keys: 2

fix: Never compute an array index without bounds-checking it against 2^32 - 2 first; if a value might legitimately be that large, use a Map or plain object keyed by string/number instead of relying on native array index semantics.
